To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the allometric trends of the shells of turtles and mammals are consistent with their protective functions.

(a) shells exhibit allometric trends in thickness and diameter, (b) the allometric trends can be explained by elastic theory, and (c) shells can be classified into three categories according to their function: protection against predator bites, protection against falling on the ground, and protection against headbutts.

(1) the thicknesses of shells of various sizes are not constant but vary with the shell's diameter according to a power law, (2) the exponent in this power law is different for shells used for different functions, and (3) these differences can be predicted from a simple scaling model based on the elastic properties of the shells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the scaling properties of shell structure and the mechanical properties that they imply, and we provide a framework to understand the evolution of shell structures.
how the mechanical properties of shells relate to the physical environment.
the scaling properties of shells, and the scaling properties of their fracture behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the shell is an evolutionary response to the environment and the forces that it is subjected to.
the allometry observed for shells is a consequence of the protective function of the shell and that the allometry is consistent with the theoretical predictions based on elastic thin-shell theory.
the allometric scaling of shells is a result of the shell's function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shell's thickness and diameter can be used to determine its protective function.
the shells used by animals for protection from different threats have different scaling relationships between their diameters and thickness.
the shell thickness is a function of shell diameter to the power 1/2 for protection from headbutting and to the power 2/5 for protection from impact with the ground.
The main takeaway from our work is that
shell thickness scales with shell diameter in such a way that it is optimal for protection against a given type of impact.

the thickness and diameter trends of shells used to protect against different threats are consistent with the physical properties of the shells, and can thus be used as indicators of the protective function of the shell.

shells used for protection against bites and headbutting exhibit a power-law relation between the shell thickness and diameter, whereas shells used for protection from ground impact exhibit a power-law trend between the shell thickness cubed and diameter cubed.
